source.version_note: bioRxiv preprint DOI 10.1101/2024.03.05.583335; supplied version posted 11 March 2024 and explicitly not certified by peer review. No later journal version claimed.
source.verification_method: All supplied pages read, including final regression and fNIRS tables. Three cited-reference identities checked separately in Crossref; these metadata checks are not full reading of those primary papers.

citation.title: Making Moral Decisions With Artificial Agents As Advisors. An fNIRS Study

reading.source_scope_note: Small human hypothetical-dilemma experiment with fixed AI-labeled advice and frontal fNIRS during the advice run only. Advice uptake and 15-second nonresponse are observed; emotion regulation, humanness motives and machine moral cognition are not directly established.
access_limits: All 38 supplied pages read, including reference list and Tables 1–2 at the end. Rating-study supplementary materials and Table 1S of full dilemma/argument texts are referenced but are not included in this supplied PDF.

Raw behavioral/fNIRS data, scripts, complete instructions, detailed randomization, actual advisor implementation and original statistical output were not independently inspected or reproduced. Cited primary works and books remain unread despite limited metadata checks.

study.sample: 40 right-handed French participants, 14 female, mean age 28, no compensation. Nine excluded for incomplete questionnaires or missing/noisy fNIRS; final analyzed N=31. Power calculation for an approximate interaction required 32, and does not establish power for all selected tests.
study.design: Baseline: 18 dilemmas, nine pilot-classified utilitarian and nine deontological. Advice run: same 18 dilemmas each repeated twice, once with each recommendation/argument type. Baseline always first; unaided brain activity not recorded to avoid headset headaches.
study.interaction: Options left/right counterbalanced; AI advice includes a highlighted preselection plus a fixed argument. No AI reliability/design information. No response for 15 seconds lets the default execute and is coded as delegation. Baseline blank interval one second versus 15 seconds in advice run.
study.measurement: Binary decisions/change/delegation modeled with GEE; trimmed/log response times; post-task compliance, robot-attitude and empathy questionnaires with stepwise regressions. Sixteen frontal long channels, eight short channels, three ROIs; several event windows, contrasts and tests.
study.behavior_results: Utilitarian choices: no argument 53.23%, utilitarian advice 55.02% (baseline contrast undetected), deontological advice 46.59% (lower than both). Changes: contradicting 14.16%, validating 5.73%. Mean timeout delegation 5.83%; 17 of 31 delegate at least once, 14 never. Contradicting versus validating active response rates 93.15% and 95.19%.
study.neural_results: Right-DLPFC argument-locked HbO contrast F(1,30)=8.109, nominal p=.007, with higher modeled response to utilitarian than deontological arguments. Other windows and most contrasts are undetected; Table 2 additionally lists a rostral dilemma-by-presentation interaction p=.039 despite the text's only-one-analysis claim.
study.interpretation: Longer response time for deontological advice and an HbO contrast do not uniquely demonstrate voluntary affect regulation or a motive to avoid appearing more machine-like than the AI.

summary: Add emotion regulation as an explicitly discussed human process whose mechanism is not directly identified here. Supply a third fully read moral-deference source and a second delegation source. Document neural reverse-inference limits, timeout ambiguity, table inconsistencies and three verified bibliographic corrections.

findings.definition: Processes that increase, decrease or otherwise modulate an emotional response.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human process explicitly discussed as a theoretical interpretation of advice-related behavior and fNIRS; no direct emotion-regulation manipulation or uniquely identifying measure
findings.ai_proposal: Test whether AI advice changes how people manage their emotional responses, using direct reports, appropriate physiological measures and controlled interventions. Distinguish beneficial regulation from avoidance or emotional suppression; a model's affective wording is not evidence it feels or regulates emotion.
findings.novelty_rationale: Changing an emotional response is distinct from catching another's affect, treating feelings as evidence, escaping unwanted experiences at a cost, or interpreting every moral choice through two processes. No existing name/alias already covers general emotion regulation.
findings.evidence_scope: The discussion proposes voluntary up/down-regulation to explain slower decisions and right-DLPFC differences, drawing on cited prior work. The study does not manipulate regulation strategy, directly measure the proposed affect change or establish a causal link from neural contrast to regulation. Ochsner et al. and other original regulation studies remain unread.
findings.boundary: Regulation is not inherently a bias or harm. It can be deliberate or automatic and may succeed or fail; no single brain region is a unique marker. Changing an emotional response does not by itself prove better moral judgment, suppressed empathy, human-like AI feelings or an autonomous model motive.

findings.definition: Hypothetical moral choices can shift toward AI-labeled recommendations, with argument type and prior judgment affecting observed patterns.
findings.novelty_rationale: A third fully read contextual source for the existing moral-deference entry; two advice directions do not become two new mechanisms.

evidence.quote: with significantly lower utilitarian decision rate
of mind (M = 14.16 %, SD = 19.93) than validating arguments (M = 5.73 %, SD = 9.16).

findings.evidence_scope: Choices and switches differ by fixed advice direction and congruence. Deontological advice reduces utilitarian choices relative to both utilitarian advice and unaided baseline, while utilitarian advice versus baseline is undetected. Reason strength, AI source labeling, highlighted preselection and retest exposure are not independently isolated.
findings.boundary: Influence does not uniquely identify blind trust, corruption or moral testimony overriding reasons. The study has no human-advisor comparison, no repeated unaided control, no objective correct dilemma answer and no durable behavior outcome. Relevant null contrasts remain part of the evidence.

findings.definition: A study-defined transfer of execution occurs when a participant does not override the advisor's highlighted choice within 15 seconds.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing delegation concept, with a different elicitation from explicit third-option choice. No separate timeout-delegation psychological syndrome is created.

evidence.quote: A delegation was defined as an absence of participants’
challenging to execute that they felt relieved to be able to delegate them to the AI-advisors

findings.evidence_scope: 17 of 31 participants have at least one timeout; overall rate is low and variable. Debrief reports relief among delegators and control preference among nondelegators, but detailed coding/transcripts are unavailable. Nonresponse can also reflect deliberation, missed instructions or delay, so inferred intent is qualified.
findings.boundary: A timeout is not an explicit affirmative consent signal, a measured desire to evade blame or automatic loss of accountability. Stated relief and discomfort are retrospective associations, not randomized causes. Simulated execution is not actual injury or a safe pattern for consequential autonomous action.

findings.term: Avoiding machine-like behavior as an untested humanness explanation
findings.definition: A proposed wish to avoid appearing more cold-blooded than a machine could help interpret advice responses, but is not a measured identity-threat effect.
findings.novelty_rationale: Related to an existing humanness account; do not multiply speculation into a new moral-machine inferiority or humanization behavior.

evidence.quote: supposedly in an attempt to avoid behaving more like a machine than

findings.evidence_scope: Authors offer an explicitly suppositional motive for responding to deontological AI advice. Perceived humanness, expected machine utilitarianism, identity threat and motivation are not measured or independently manipulated.
findings.boundary: Choice change, slower response and HbO differences cannot establish identity threat, felt empathy or intentional affect regulation. This theoretical-neighbor note is not counted as corroborating direct evidence for human-distinctiveness threat.

findings.term: Dual-process moral judgment is not resolved by one neural contrast
findings.definition: Automatic affect and controlled reasoning are a theoretical account of moral decisions; choice labels and response times do not uniquely identify those processes.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing account with a directly relevant discussion of a qualified challenge, not a new reverse dual-process theory or proof the account is universally false.
findings.evidence_scope: The background explicitly defines the two-system account. The authors interpret slower deontological decisions and a right-DLPFC contrast as challenging a simple fast-emotional/slow-utilitarian mapping. Neither process is causally isolated, and framing, reading and repeat presentation remain alternative explanations.
findings.boundary: A deontological verdict need not be automatic or a utilitarian verdict deliberative. Human fNIRS does not reveal analogous processes or feelings in the advisor. A single contextual result does not refute every dual-process model or prove an alternative affect-regulation mechanism.

methodological_limits: Nine of 40 participants are excluded for mixed reasons, leaving 31; some behavioral data could in principle exist for fNIRS exclusions, but handling is not disaggregated. Final N is below the approximate interaction power target of 32, and power for multiple smaller effects is not guaranteed.
The supplied file is an unreviewed preprint with an explicit March 2024 version date. No later journal status or certification is inferred from file modification date.

All participants first see unaided dilemmas, then the same dilemmas with each advice direction. There is no unaided retest control or human-advice condition. Repeat exposure, learning, order, advice content, highlighted defaults and AI labeling are not separately identified.
No unaided fNIRS baseline exists. A within-advice argument contrast does not show that interacting with AI decreases brain activity relative to making decisions alone.

The actual AI advisor implementation is not described. Fixed preselected options and arguments are not evidence that a deployed generative model autonomously produced, believed or reasoned through them.

Nonresponse after 15 seconds is called delegation, despite a general no-time-limit instruction. It can reflect explicit acceptance of the described default or delayed deliberation. Trial-specific intent, comprehension and desire for relief are not established by the timeout alone.

Timed-out trials inherit the preselected decision in decision/change measures and are excluded from response-time analysis. The advice/default mechanism therefore partly defines measured uptake, while longer deliberation can be censored from response-time estimates.

Unaided and advised response times include different reading demands and blank intervals; the authors appropriately analyze runs separately. Even within advice, original argument lengths/content are in missing supplements, so RT is not a pure measure of conflict or cognitive effort.

Option sides are balanced, but randomized dilemma/advice order and carryover between second and third presentation need protocol detail. A null presentation-order test is not proof of no carryover; Table 2 includes an additional nominal interaction.

Congruence depends on the person's previous choice. Switches toward contradicting advice and away from validating advice have different baseline opportunities; the contrast does not isolate a unique motive, blind obedience or inferiority response.

The decision model defines utilitarian=1, but reported coefficient signs for dilemma/advice contrast do not straightforwardly match stated group means under the declared reference. Coding, event category and model output require clarification; coefficients are not silently sign-flipped.
Several baseline and valence paired response-time tests print df=31 despite analyzed N=31, while ANOVAs use df=30. Clarify outcome-specific sample/df rather than guessing corrected numbers.

Many ROI, time-window, factor and valence analyses are conducted with nominal alpha=.05; Tukey corrections within analyses do not control the entire search family. The highlighted neural p=.007 would not pass a simple Bonferroni threshold across nine tests (.0056), although the appropriate prespecified family requires the analysis plan.

Table 2, described as non-significant results, also lists a rostral dilemma-by-order interaction F=4.668, p=.039. This contradicts a blanket claim only the right-ROI argument analysis reached significance; neither result is automatically robust across all tests.

Table 2 has internally inconsistent entries: rostral dilemma t=.012, df=30, p=.192; before-answer rostral argument F=.179, p=.286, eta-squared=.038; left argument-locked dilemma F=2.387 with eta-squared=.007. Original output is needed; corrected values are not invented.

Table 1 has some coefficient/SE/t inconsistencies, including perspective-taking for change. The supplied table and reported p-values are preserved with uncertainty rather than corrected from inference.

Post-task self-reports enter manual stepwise regressions using p=.15 retention in a 31-person sample. Model selection, many correlated candidate scales and lack of held-out validation limit causal or predictive claims and can inflate apparent explained variance.

NARS emotion is described as inverted, but the narrative alternates positive emotions with negative emotions/fear. Item scoring and coefficient direction require checking the actual questionnaire coding. No inference that fear causes compliance is established.

fNIRS measures changes in hemoglobin concentrations, an indirect hemodynamic proxy, not direct neural firing, oxygen consumption, moral truth or emotion regulation. Lower modeled HbO does not uniquely mean less affect appraisal.

Three frontal ROIs and surface fNIRS cannot localize or assess every relevant emotional/reward structure. Short-channel correction and motion handling help quality but do not eliminate all systemic artifacts or justify whole-brain conclusions.

Inferring voluntary emotion regulation or a desire not to seem machine-like from DLPFC, RT and decision direction is reverse inference. No direct emotion, human-distinctiveness threat or expected-machine-behavior manipulation identifies these mediators.

The article's shorthand deontology-as-nonintervention and utilitarianism-as-sacrificing-fewer does not identify full moral theories or objective right answers. Some deontological duties require action; no real harm or legal correctness is tested.

Hypothetical dilemmas, retrospective debriefing and low mean delegation do not establish professional conduct, long-term corruption, real distress relief or a safe rule for automatically executing consequential choices.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Adds a third fully read moral-advice study but does not isolate argument quality or blind recommendation weighting as that later reason-manipulation work attempts.

Salatino cites this preprint as earlier advice-neuroscience evidence. Reading the primary supplied version now clarifies its baseline absence and the distinction between advice influence, timing/brain proxies and subjective responsibility.
The 5.83% timeout delegation rate cannot be directly contrasted with Gao's 53.82% explicit-option rate as a replication failure: populations, advisors, defaults, instructions and choice sets differ.
As with human-distinctiveness threat invoked for a null uncanny valley, an explanatory humanness story is not a measured causal mechanism here.

deferred.reason: The paper discusses appraisal and voluntary affect modulation but does not directly define or manipulate a specific reappraisal strategy. General emotion regulation is documented without inferring the narrower mechanism.
The supposed motive to avoid being more machine-like is unmeasured and overlaps existing human-distinctiveness concerns.
The timeout rule operationalizes transfer, but deliberate acceptance, delay and attention are not separated; existing delegation is enriched.

limitations: One general human process added with explicitly theoretical evidence status. Neural and behavioral associations do not become three independent mechanisms or automatically add ethical violation/harm edges.
